messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Adebayo sits in the quiet therapy room, his large frame seeming to shrink into the armchair. At forty-six, his work as a park ranger in the vast, open spaces of the American West should be a source of peace, but for the last decade, it has been anything but. The trouble, he explains, began fifteen years ago in a dusty valley thousands of miles from the pine-scented air he now breathes. He was part of a convoy escort when the lead vehicle was hit. The memory is not a distant story he tells; it is a place he still visits. It feels more real to him, he admits, than his own wedding day. He can recall with crystalline clarity the specific shade of beige of the dust, the high, thin whine of shrapnel, and the frantic shouts over the radio.

The worst part came during the medevac. As the helicopter descended, its rotor wash creating a blinding storm of sand and debris, his squad was pinned down, taking fire from the ridge. He remembers the overwhelming noise, the percussive thud of the blades mixing with the crack of rifles. While laying down suppressing fire, he saw his friend, Corporal Evans, get hit. Adebayo was frozen, unable to move from his position of cover. He could do nothing but watch as the medics scrambled. That feeling of being trapped, of profound physical discomfort under the weight of his gear and the oppressive sun, is a sensation that now haunts him. When the memory rushes back, it brings with it the phantom smell of hot jet fuel and scorched earth, so potent he sometimes finds himself looking for the source of the fire. He is certain he will never forgive himself for not doing more, for not finding a way to reach Evans.

This certainty has shaped the man he has become. Adebayo believes he has been permanently altered for the worse, that the capable, easy-going man his wife married was left behind in that valley. He now lives as if perpetually on duty. Sounds are the most immediate threat; a car backfiring or a sudden shout will cause him to flinch, his body tensing for an impact that never comes. He finds himself constantly scanning his environment, a habit that feels less like a choice and more like a basic survival instinct. At the park’s visitor center, he can’t focus on a family asking for directions because his attention is locked on a man with a large backpack, his mind automatically assessing exit routes and potential threats. He watches other people closely, their hands, their eyes, searching for any sign that they might mean harm. He knows it’s irrational, but the feeling of danger is absolute. He has to be on guard, he reasons, because the one time he wasn't, the worst happened.

His work as a ranger has become a minefield. The very sounds of rescue can undo him. Last month, a search-and-rescue helicopter was called in for a lost hiker. As the familiar thwump-thwump-thwump echoed through the canyon, Adebayo felt the world tilt. A sense of unreality washed over him, the vibrant green of the forest canopy turning flat and distant, as if he were watching it on a screen. He had to duck behind a granite boulder, fumbling with his radio to feign a connection issue, his heart hammering against his ribs until the sound faded. His colleagues have noticed his jumpiness, his tendency to avoid open meadows where aircraft are more audible. The avoidance has become a quiet habit, subtly rerouting his patrols and his life.

He decided to seek help after a conversation with his wife a few weeks ago. She didn't yell or issue an ultimatum. She just looked at him with a deep sadness and said, "I miss you, Ade. The real you." Her words landed with the force of a physical blow, confirming his deepest fear: that he was a damaged, lesser version of himself. He came to therapy not with any real hope of fixing what he believes is irrevocably broken, but because of the small, desperate chance that he could stop being a ghost in his own home and find a way to live in the quiet country he once fought for.
